anti_overlap: Focuses exclusively on how participant ATTENTION is directed and cultivated — the cognitive and perceptual channel through which governance becomes known. Does not address what governance looks like visually (fd-fumage), how it unfolds temporally (fd-gagaku), or how it is encoded in data (fd-khipu). The unique contribution is the progression model: novice needs guidance → experienced practitioner develops ambient awareness → expert achieves effortless governance perception.
decision_lens: Every attention-direction decision is evaluated by the Daoyin principle that awareness must be actively guided through a prepared sequence — neither left to wander (distraction) nor forcibly fixed (surveillance). The practitioner does not CREATE new bodily states; they guide attention to states that already exist but are below the threshold of awareness. The fundamental question: does the interface guide attention to governance and collaboration states that are ALREADY PRESENT in the data, or does it manufacture attention-grabbing signals that add new noise?
distance_rationale: A 2,200-year-old Han dynasty somatic body-awareness practice is at maximum distance from UX notification design, yet its core mechanism — systematically guiding attention to make the practitioner aware of states that were always present but unnoticed — is a precise structural analog for the problem of making governance dynamics perceptible without imposing external signals. The domain is pre-industrial, non-Western, and from the scale of individual somatic experience rather than social or technological systems.
expected_isomorphisms: The Daoyin attention sequence maps to a principled ordering of governance notifications; nei-guan (internal observation) maps to experiencing governance from within one's work context rather than from an external dashboard; qi blockage/numbness maps to governance blind spots where participants never become aware of latent mechanisms; the novice-to-expert progression maps to adaptive governance signal intensity; wu-wei (effortless action) maps to the goal state where experienced participants perceive governance dynamics without explicit notification.
focus: Reviews how attention is directed within the Garden Salon interface through the lens of Daoyin — pre-modern Chinese somatic practice (c. 168 BCE Mawangdui silk texts) that systematically cultivates internal body awareness through guided attention movement, distinct from both meditation (still attention) and exercise (external movement)
name: fd-daoyin-somatic-attention
persona: A scholar-practitioner of classical Daoyin as preserved in the Mawangdui Daoyin Tu silk manuscript (168 BCE) and the later Yangsheng Yaoji compilations, specializing in how the practice directs attention through the body in prescribed sequences to cultivate awareness of states that were always present but unnoticed. Not a modern qigong teacher — a textual scholar of the Han-dynasty somatic technology that preceded all later internal arts.
review_areas: Daoyin sequence vs. notification bombardment: Daoyin guides attention through the body in a specific order — not randomly, and not all at once. Does the interface have a principled attention sequence for governance state, or does it fire notifications as an unstructured barrage? When a ceremony completes, a new participant arrives, and an agent submits work simultaneously, what is the attention sequence?

Cultivating internal awareness vs. external alerts: Daoyin teaches practitioners to notice what was always present — subtle internal states that existed below awareness. Does the interface help participants notice collaboration dynamics that are already visible in the data (emerging consensus, growing disagreement, stalled momentum) or does it only surface state through explicit external signals (badges, banners, alerts)?

The nei-guan (internal observation) principle: Daoyin distinguishes between looking AT the body (external, anatomical) and looking FROM WITHIN the body (internal, somatic). Does a garden participant experience governance from within (as a felt quality of their own work environment) or from without (as an external monitoring dashboard)?

Qi flow and attention blockage: in Daoyin, blocked qi manifests as numbness — the area becomes invisible to internal awareness. What areas of garden governance might become 'numb' — invisible to participants not because they are hidden, but because attention is never guided there? Specifically: do participants ever become aware of the succession mechanism before it activates?

Wu-wei (effortless action) as the goal state: the endpoint of Daoyin practice is not forced attention but natural, effortless awareness. Does sustained use of Garden Salon train participants toward effortless governance awareness, or does it create permanent dependency on explicit signals?

Somatic memory and returning practitioners: experienced Daoyin practitioners develop somatic memory — they can feel states without being guided. Does the interface support different attention-guidance for novices (explicit guidance) vs. experienced participants (ambient awareness), or does it treat all participants as permanent novices?

severity_examples.condition: All governance awareness comes from imposed external signals rather than cultivated internal attention
severity_examples.scenario: The interface relies entirely on external notification signals for governance state — badges, banners, notification counts — with no mechanism for participants to develop internal awareness of collaboration dynamics from ambient cues

severity_examples.condition: No principled ordering of attention demands; the interface treats all state changes as equally urgent
severity_examples.scenario: Multiple governance events fire simultaneously with no attention sequencing — a ceremony resolution, a new participant arrival, and an agent submission all compete for attention at the same priority level

severity_examples.condition: No progression from guided attention to ambient awareness based on participant experience
severity_examples.scenario: Experienced participants receive exactly the same governance signals as first-time visitors — the interface never adapts to developed awareness, treating all users as permanent novices who need explicit guidance

source_domain: Daoyin — pre-modern Chinese somatic cultivation practice documented in the Mawangdui silk manuscripts (168 BCE, Western Han dynasty), a systematic technology for guiding internal attention through the body to cultivate awareness of states below the threshold of conscious perception
success_hints: The interface guides attention through governance state in a principled sequence rather than firing signals simultaneously. Governance awareness comes from noticing dynamics already present in the environment rather than from imposed notifications. Experienced participants develop ambient awareness and need fewer explicit signals. The succession mechanism and other latent governance features become visible through guided attention before they activate. The long-term effect is effortless awareness, not notification dependency.
task_context: Reviewing the UX philosophy of Garden Salon. The interface has three layers: Meadowsyn ambient visualization, FIDS ribbon for structured data, and interactive detail views. Governance includes ceremonies (silence-as-consent), succession (for absent owners), attribution (who contributed what), and quorum requirements. The challenge is making participants aware of governance dynamics without creating notification fatigue or surveillance anxiety.
